title: Re-tell Lecture: urban heat islands
prompt: You will hear a lecture. After listening to the lecture, in 10 seconds, please speak into the microphone and retell what you have just heard in your own words. You will have 40 seconds to give your response.

stimulus.text: A short lecture on why cities are warmer than the countryside around them.

transcript: Cities are consistently warmer than the countryside around them, and the difference can reach several degrees on a still summer night. The reason is mostly material. Asphalt and concrete absorb heat through the day and release it slowly after dark, while the countryside cools quickly. Add waste heat from vehicles and air conditioning, and remove the trees whose shade and evaporation once did the cooling, and you have what is called an urban heat island. The remedies are unglamorous but effective: more tree cover, lighter roof surfaces, and open water where a city can afford the space.

title: Summarize Written Text: reopening buried rivers
prompt: Read the passage below and summarise it using one sentence. Type your response in the box at the bottom of the screen. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well it presents the key points in the passage.

stimulus.text:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners treated rivers as obstacles. Watercourses that had shaped settlement for centuries were culverted, paved over and turned into roads, on the reasoning that a buried river took up no land and carried away waste without complaint.

That reasoning has not aged well. Buried rivers still flood, but they do so through drains and basements rather than across a floodplain, and the damage is more expensive. Covered channels also lose the cooling that open water provides, which matters more in each successive hot summer.

A number of cities have now reversed the work. Seoul removed an elevated motorway to uncover the Cheonggyecheon, and found that surrounding streets ran several degrees cooler. The projects are slow and costly, and their benefits accrue over decades rather than electoral cycles, which is the main reason more cities have not attempted them.
